analysis.one_liner: Cuts the corporate tax rate to 28% while closing offshore profit-shifting loopholes and oil industry tax breaks.
analysis.headline: A single senator introduced the bill with no cosponsors, and it died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have lowered the top corporate income tax rate from 35% to 28% over five years, while paying for that cut by closing a long list of tax breaks that let companies shift profits and jobs offshore. It would also have ended the oil industry's percentage depletion allowance, tightened rules on foreign tax credits and tax shelters, and made permanent expanded write-offs for small businesses. It never got past the committee stage.
analysis.who_benefits: United States corporations would pay a lower tax rate, and small businesses would get permanent expanded expensing and a bigger domestic production deduction. Workers could benefit indirectly if the anti-offshoring provisions kept jobs and tax revenue in the country.

how_it_helps.text: Phases the maximum corporate tax rate down from 35% to 28% between 2009 and 2013, lowering taxes on profitable companies.
Treats foreign corporations managed and controlled primarily in the US as domestic corporations, so they cannot escape US tax by booking ownership abroad.
Limits treaty-based withholding benefits on payments among foreign-controlled related companies, a common channel for shifting profits out of the US.
Codifies the economic substance doctrine and adds penalties, up to 40% for undisclosed transactions, on tax deals with no real business purpose.
Makes permanent the expanded small business expensing allowance and raises the domestic production deduction to 12% for businesses other than C corporations.

analysis.who_pays: Multinational companies using offshore structures, oil and gas companies (which lose the percentage depletion allowance), tax shelter promoters facing new penalties, and expatriate taxpayers who would lose the refundable child tax credit. Corporations with no offshore structures would get the rate cut without those costs.

drawbacks.text: Cutting the corporate rate from 35% to 28% would reduce federal revenue that funds public services, unless the loophole closers fully offset it — an outcome the bill's backers assumed but that depends on hard-to-estimate behavioral responses from companies.
The bill repeals the 3% withholding requirement on government payments to vendors, which the 2005 law created to catch vendors who underpay their taxes — removing a compliance backstop.

The domestic production deduction is increased but limited to businesses other than C corporations, so large manufacturers get the rate cut while losing that deduction, and the net effect on any given company varies widely.
The bill extends the 6.2% federal unemployment tax rate through 2018 rather than letting it fall, keeping a payroll tax in place that otherwise would have dropped.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a classic corporate tax trade: a lower headline rate in exchange for closing loopholes. The anti-offshoring provisions and shelter penalties genuinely serve the public interest in keeping jobs and tax revenue onshore, and the small business provisions help domestic employers. But the rate cut is a large, permanent benefit that flows to all profitable corporations regardless of whether they keep jobs in America, while the offsetting revenue comes from narrower crackdowns whose yields are uncertain. Expats lose a child credit and government vendors lose a withholding rule along the way. On balance it is a serious attempt at revenue-conscious corporate reform, but its benefits reach ordinary people only indirectly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator George Voinovich of Ohio introduced the bill on June 19, 2008, near the end of the 110th Congress.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no committee action followed.
Not a single senator cosponsored the bill.
The bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that benefit from the current rules — multinationals shifting profits offshore, oil companies claiming percentage depletion, and promoters of tax shelters — kept every advantage the bill would have taken away. The corporate rate stayed at 35%, so nothing changed for anyone.

for.name: Sen. George Voinovich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: The 99 other sitting senators
against.what_they_did: None of the other 99 senators signed on as a cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the bill's only sponsor was a Republican senator who attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.note: The bill tightens the foreign tax credit rules, treats US-managed foreign corporations as domestic, limits treaty benefits on related-party payments, and taxes deferred compensation paid by tax-haven entities. These provisions target the structures that let companies book profits abroad instead of paying US tax, which means less revenue and fewer incentives to move work offshore.

The bill repeals the percentage depletion allowance after 2008 and sets a fair-market-value standard for foreign oil and gas extraction income, ending a decades-old tax break for extractive industries.

They would gain a phased rate cut to 28%, but the bill repeals lower-of-cost-or-market inventory accounting, lengthens goodwill amortization from 15 to 20 years, and limits excess interest deductions. A company's net result depends heavily on how much it uses the targeted breaks.
Permanent $125,000 expensing, permanent software expensing, and a bigger 12% domestic production deduction give smaller domestic firms permanent tax advantages that had been scheduled to lapse.
Codifying the economic substance doctrine with 20-40% penalties and no reasonable-cause exception for shelter transactions raises the cost of selling tax-motivated deals.
Repealing the 3% withholding on government payments to vendors spares contractors the cash-flow cost of prepaying tax, but removes a mechanism designed to catch vendors underpaying their own taxes.
